Use case: AI accessibility checks and alt text
Tool categories: Design and whiteboard tools | General AI assistants
Description: AI is used to make prototypes and generated interfaces more accessible: drafting alternative text for images, and checking or steering generated UI code against WCAG rules such as color contrast, labels and alt attributes. In the A11yn research system, generated web UI code is rendered and scanned with the axe-core accessibility engine, and the violations are used as a penalty to train the code model to produce more accessible output. NN/g's practitioner FAQ lists alternative-text generation among the tasks where AI is 'genuinely useful' as a first draft. It sits in both making (accessible generation) and evaluating (automated checks) of the artifact. The GenUI diary study of 37 professionals concluded that generative UI tools must address practical considerations such as accessibility and standards.
Acceptability reason: Researchers show AI can reduce violations and NN/g accepts AI alt-text as a first draft, but evidence that generated UIs omit accessibility features means human and tool-based audits remain required.
Advantages:
• Accessibility can be systematically optimized within code-generating LLMs using WCAG-based rewards (A11yn authors, arXiv 2025)
• AI is useful for first-draft alternative text (NN/g, UX Writing FAQs)
Disadvantages:
• LLMs omit key accessibility elements such as alt text, semantic landmarks and labeled form controls (A11yn authors, summarizing prior studies, arXiv 2025)
• Generative UI tools still fall short on accessibility and standards (Chen, Knearem & Li, GenUI study, DIS '25)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 0 built-in tools, 1 independent report → low.
Independent reports: Supercharge accessibility with Sidekick from Stark (Tom Green, UX Collective) — https://uxdesign.cc/supercharge-accessibility-with-sidekick-from-stark-dd0f66153d32

Resource 2: UX Writing: FAQs from Practitioners

Use case: AI design critique of UI screens
Description: Instead of checking fixed rules, the AI writes open-ended design feedback on a UI screenshot, the way a senior designer might in a critique session, pointing to specific regions and giving quality ratings. The input is a screenshot, optionally with expert example critiques; the model produces comments with bounding boxes and scores; the designer uses them to revise. It sits in evaluation, as a substitute for peer critique when no human reviewer is available. The UIST '24 UICrit dataset collected 3,059 critiques and ratings for 983 mobile UIs from seven experienced designers, and using it in prompts produced a 55% performance gain in LLM-generated feedback. Even so, the authors and later benchmark work (PerceptUI, 2026) report that human designer critiques remain stronger than every LLM method tested.
Acceptability reason: The HCI researchers who built and benchmarked these systems present them as helpful supplements but explicitly below human critique quality, so output should be treated as a prompt for reflection, not a verdict.
Advantages:
• Gives instant feedback when human critique is unavailable; expert-example prompting improved quality by 55% (Duan et al., UICrit, UIST '24)
• Feedback is tied to specific screen regions, making it easier to act on (Duan et al., UIST '24)
Disadvantages:
• Still far from the quality of human design critiques (Duan et al., UICrit, UIST '24)
• Few-shot imitation of critiques yields shallow comments that miss why an issue matters (PerceptUI authors, arXiv 2026)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 0 built-in tools, 0 independent reports → insufficient evidence. Not fully re-verified in the October 2026 update; re-check in Run 3.
Resource 1: UICrit: Enhancing Automated Design Evaluation with a UI Critique Dataset
Resource 2: PerceptUI: LLM Agents as Human-Aligned Synthetic Users for UI/UX Evaluation

Description: Real participants test a designed prototype while AI handles parts of the moderator's job, such as asking follow-up questions in response to what the participant did or said, and then summarizing the sessions. The researcher uploads a prototype (including AI-generated ones from Figma Make, Lovable or Bolt) and sets tasks; the platform's AI probes participants and drafts reports; the output is recordings, highlights and themes. It sits in prototype evaluation with real people, unlike previously mapped AI-moderated interviews (Research), which explore people's lives rather than an artifact. Maze lists an AI moderator and AI follow-up questions alongside prototype testing and quotes a customer saying that within a few hours they had multiple participant responses, video highlights and a clear report. Figma's guide cites its 2025 AI report: 24% of designers and 40% of developers already use AI during testing.
Acceptability reason: The only sources found are vendors, which frame AI as automating routine moderation and reporting while researchers keep control; without independent evaluation, use with human oversight.
Advantages:
• Fast turnaround: responses, highlights and a shareable report within hours (Maze customer quote – vendor claim)
• Automates routine tasks like transcription, tagging and reporting so testing keeps pace with faster prototyping (Figma AI usability testing guide – vendor)
Disadvantages:
• No independent evaluation of AI moderation quality in prototype tests was found; all evidence is vendor material (gap noted in this scan)
• AI UX tools generally fail to disclose accuracy or limitations (Baymard cofounders via NN/g, Kate Moran, 2026)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 1 built-in tool, 0 independent reports → low.
Resource 1: AI usability testing guide: Modern workflow and tools
Resource 2: User Testing Platform for Product Teams | Maze

Tool categories: Prototyping and coding tools | Research prototypes
Description: An AI agent actually clicks through a running prototype or website, gathers evidence of what happens, and writes a structured UX report with prioritized fixes; in some setups a second AI agent then edits the code to apply them. The input is a live URL or runnable prototype (plus optional personas and tasks); the agent explores, records screenshots and actions, and outputs ranked recommendations or a repaired interface. It sits in evaluation of interactive prototypes, aiming to remove manual review of long simulation logs. AMUSER ran 145 simulations on 10 real finance and fashion websites and produced 1,200 recommendations; its multimodal version scored NDCG@3 0.758 versus 0.359 for text-only simulation, at 89% lower simulation cost. UXBench tested eight frontier models and found that models differ meaningfully in how actionable their critiques are, judged by whether a fixed repair agent could improve the interface.
Acceptability reason: The researchers developing these systems (UCL, Notre Dame) present them as promising but unsaturated, with quality varying by model and interface type, so outputs need human validation.
Advantages:
• Automatically turns interaction traces into prioritized recommendations, beating static analysis and text-only simulation at much lower cost (Chowdhury et al., AMUSER, arXiv 2026)
• Measures critique quality by whether it leads to real interface improvement, not just plausibility (Wang et al., UXBench, arXiv 2026)
Disadvantages:
• UX judging is 'neither saturated nor one-dimensional'; models vary in reliability across fixtures and surface types (Wang et al., UXBench, arXiv 2026)
• Giving visual inputs at the recommendation stage can modestly degrade quality (Chowdhury et al., AMUSER, arXiv 2026)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 0 built-in tools, 0 independent reports → insufficient evidence.

Use case: LLM agents as simulated test users
Description: AI 'personas' are generated in bulk and each one is turned into an agent that tries to complete tasks on a designed website or prototype, producing data that resembles a usability test. In UXAgent, a persona generator feeds an LLM agent that operates a real Chrome browser; outputs include action traces, reasoning traces, video recordings and an interface for 'interviewing' the agent about its choices. The stated purpose is to let UX researchers pilot and debug their usability study design before running it with real people, not to replace them. This differs from the previously mapped 'synthetic users replacing participants' (Research), because here agents operate a designed artifact. In UXAgent's own evaluation, five UX researchers reviewed data from 60 agent personas on a shopping site; they called it 'very helpful' but said the behavior was 'not like real humans' and 'real human [users] won't think like that'.
Acceptability reason: HCI researchers building these systems see value for piloting test plans at scale, while UX researchers in their own evaluations voiced concerns and follow-up work stresses that agent behaviour needs explicit alignment with real humans.
Advantages:
• Can generate thousands of simulated participants to iterate on a usability study's design before recruiting humans (Lu et al., UXAgent, CHI EA '25)
• Produces qualitative, quantitative and video outputs for researchers to inspect (Lu et al., CHI EA '25)
Disadvantages:
• UX researchers said agent behavior was 'not like real humans' and expressed concerns about LLM agents in UX studies (Lu et al., CHI EA '25)
• Prior simulation work is largely text-only, evaluated on a single e-commerce site, and requires costly manual review of traces (Chowdhury et al., AMUSER, arXiv 2026)
• One UXAgent run was terminated after its context grew to more than 400k tokens from raw HTML parsing (Chowdhury et al., AMUSER, arXiv 2026)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 0 built-in tools, 0 independent reports → insufficient evidence.

Resource 2: Automatic multimodal UX improvement recommendations from LLM agent user simulations (AMUSER)

Description: An AI checks a mockup, prototype or live page against a written list of usability guidelines (heuristics) and reports where the design breaks them, with suggested fixes. In the CHI '24 system, the designer selects guidelines in a Figma plugin; the plugin sends a text representation of the UI plus the guidelines to GPT-4; violations are shown as constructive suggestions linked to the design, and the designer revises and reruns. It sits in evaluation, as a quick check before or between human reviews and tests. The authors assessed it on 51 UIs with three expert raters and compared it with 12 design experts doing the same evaluation. By contrast, Baymard's test of ChatGPT-4 on 12 webpages against 6 human UX professionals found only 20% accuracy, an 80% false-positive rate, and discovery of only 14–26% of issues.
Acceptability reason: The CHI '24 authors see a useful supplement for designers, whereas Baymard's cofounders (on NN/g's podcast) argue that generic AI audit tools are too inaccurate (50–70%) and should be bought only with a documented accuracy near human level.
Advantages:
• Provides instant guideline-based feedback inside the designer's Figma workflow when human evaluators are unavailable (Duan, Warner, Li & Hartmann, CHI '24)
• A narrowly scoped, research-grounded approach claims 95% accuracy versus human auditors on 154 e-commerce heuristics (Baymard Institute – vendor claim)
Disadvantages:
• GPT-4 UX audits showed 20% accuracy and an 80% false-positive error rate (Baymard Institute)
• Most AI UX tools don't disclose accuracy; measured tools ranged 50–70% (Christian & Jamie Holst, Baymard, via NN/g, Kate Moran, 2026)
• LLMs hallucinate and struggle with hierarchical UI structure represented as text (Duan et al., CHI '24)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 0 built-in tools, 0 independent reports → insufficient evidence. Not fully re-verified in the October 2026 update; re-check in Run 3.

Tool categories: Analytics and feedback tools | Design and whiteboard tools
Description: AI predicts where people's eyes will go on a design, producing a colored 'heatmap' without recruiting anyone for an eye-tracking study. The designer uploads a mockup, screenshot or URL; a model trained on past eye-tracking data (or a general vision-language model) estimates visual attention; the output is a heatmap and often scores for elements such as CTAs. It sits in evaluation of static artifacts, typically pre-launch, as a fast stand-in for real eye tracking. The independent UIGaze preprint (2026) compared nine vision-language models with real gaze data from 62 people on 1,980 UI screens: the best reached only moderate alignment (correlation 0.408 at 7 seconds, 0.227 at 1 second), capturing exploratory gaze rather than first fixations, and did worse on dense mobile layouts. Vendors, by contrast, claim 90–96% (Attention Insight) or 94% (Brainsight) accuracy, figures that are self-reported.
Acceptability reason: Vendors claim near-eye-tracking accuracy, but independent researchers find only moderate alignment with human gaze on interfaces and disagreement between tools, so credible sources do not support treating heatmaps as a substitute for testing.
Advantages:
• Instant, participant-free predictions suited to speed and pre-launch checks (Brainsight – vendor claim)
• General vision-language models are 'useful, if imperfect' for early design reviews (Song, Lee & Seo, UIGaze, arXiv 2026)
Disadvantages:
• Only moderate alignment with real gaze on UIs, weakest for first glances and mobile screens (Song, Lee & Seo, UIGaze, arXiv 2026)
• Commercial tools disagree with each other about hotspots on the same images (Journal of Eye Movement Research, 2026)
• Accuracy figures are self-reported; Attention Insight itself notes a competitor lacks independent third-party validation (Attention Insight comparison page)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 0 built-in tools, 0 independent reports → insufficient evidence. Not fully re-verified in the October 2026 update; re-check in Run 3.

Description: In a diary study, participants log experiences over days or weeks. DiaryHelper takes text, photo, audio or video entries, converts media to text, and uses GPT-3.5 to predict the time, location, emotion, people and activity, which the participant confirms or edits. It sits inside fieldwork and feeds later interviews. In a two-week CHI 2024 study with 12 participants, it reduced recording burden and helped participants recall more detail.
Acceptability reason: The authors (Li et al., HKUST) restricted the AI to fixed label sets to limit hallucination and gave each participant a private channel.
Advantages:
• Lower recording burden and higher willingness to record (Li et al.)
• Richer recall of emotions and activities in follow-up interviews (Li et al.)
Disadvantages:
• Small, young, mostly male sample on one topic (Li et al.)
• Hallucination risk needs constrained outputs (Li et al.)

Description: An AI interviewer is a synthetic voice or chatbot that runs an interview with no human present. The researcher uploads a guide; the AI asks the questions, probes when answers are short, and returns transcripts and summaries. It replaces the moderator during fieldwork, so many interviews can run in parallel. NN/g ran 10 research leaders through Marvin and UserFlix: sessions lasted 13 to 56 minutes, and only 3 of 10 said the conversation felt natural.
Acceptability reason: NN/g (Rosala) limits it to structured interviews. Wuttke et al. (LMU) found data quality comparable to human interviewers. Cuevas et al. (CMU and Microsoft Research) found poor richness. Vendors claim near parity.
Advantages:
• Scale and flexible scheduling (NN/g)
• Data quality comparable to human interviewers in a controlled study (Wuttke et al.)
• Summaries made participants feel heard (NN/g)
Disadvantages:
• Follows the script rather than the insight; sycophantic praise (Rosala, NN/g)
• Responses rarely capture specific motives or personal examples (Cuevas et al.)
• Some participants withheld information over privacy worries (NN/g)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 3 built-in tools, 2 independent reports → medium.

Description: Open-ended survey answers are often short, so an LLM chatbot embedded in the survey asks one follow-up probe. The participant's answer goes in; the chatbot generates a probe; a richer answer comes out. It sits in data collection at scale. Jacobsen et al. Description: A digital twin is an AI model built from one real person's survey or interview data that predicts how that person would answer. Past answers go in; predicted answers to skipped or new questions come out. It sits in data collection, for example to fill gaps in long surveys. NN/g's Raluca Budiu reviews a study in which twins filled missing survey answers with 78% accuracy but managed only 67% on new questions.
Acceptability reason: Budiu (NN/g) finds twins promising for missing data, unlike synthetic users, but flags demographic bias and unresolved consent questions; vendors market them as customer replicas.

• Population-level correlation of r=0.98 when filling missing data (Budiu, NN/g)

Disadvantages:
• Less accurate for non-white and lower-socioeconomic respondents (Budiu, NN/g)

Description: Synthetic users are AI-generated 'participants' that answer interview questions in place of real people. The researcher specifies a user group and goal; the tool invents profiles and produces interview transcripts. It is marketed as a replacement for fieldwork ('User research. Without the users.'). NN/g reran three of its real studies with Synthetic Users and ChatGPT and found the answers shallow and overly favorable.
Acceptability reason: NN/g, the CHI 2025 'Simulacrum of Stories' paper and the CHI 2023 Hämäläinen paper all say findings must come from or be validated with real people. Synthetic Users cofounder Hugo Alves told NN/g, 'You're never gonna stop talking to real people.'
Advantages:
• Believable answers produced cheaply and quickly (Hämäläinen et al.)
• Researchers were surprised to see narratives similar to real data (Kapania et al.)
Disadvantages:
• Shallow, overly favorable feedback (NN/g)
• Forecloses consent and agency, lacks palpability: the 'surrogate effect' (Kapania et al.)
• Teams may get comfortable and skip real research (NN/g)

Description: AI sorts free-text survey answers (such as 'what frustrated you?') into themes and counts how many fall in each. Description: While a UX evaluator watches a usability-test recording, an AI assistant suggests possible usability problems and answers questions about the session. Description: Instead of a second human, an LLM independently codes the same data so the researcher can compare agreement and discuss disagreements. Human-coded data and the same raw data go to the AI; agreement statistics (such as kappa) show where the two diverge. It sits at the validation step of coding, where teams normally check inter-rater reliability. MeasuringU found ChatGPT-4 agreement with humans (kappa .632) only slightly below human-human agreement in 2023; in its September 2026 rerun, human-to-ChatGPT-5.6 agreement (0.749) was statistically indistinguishable from human-to-human agreement (0.704, p = .475).
Acceptability reason: MeasuringU and academic studies support it with multiple runs and human adjudication because LLM output is non-deterministic.
Advantages:
• Human-comparable kappa with near-perfect self-consistency for ChatGPT-5.6 (MeasuringU, Schiavone, Sundberg & Sauro, 2026)
• Strong inter-rater reliability with humans (K = 0.84) on excerpt identification (Human vs LLM TA study, 2025)
Disadvantages:
• Outputs are not deterministic; a single run cannot be trusted (MeasuringU, Lewis)
• Newer model over-subdivided themes (15.6 vs 13.3 human themes on average), risking fragmentation of macro themes (MeasuringU, 2026)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 0 built-in tools, 0 independent reports → insufficient evidence. Not fully re-verified in the October 2026 update; re-check in Run 3.

Description: The researcher gives the AI a fixed codebook and asks it to label each passage with the right code. Codebook definitions and text segments go in; the LLM returns a code per segment, optionally with its reasoning. It is used after a codebook exists, to apply it consistently across many interviews or comments. In RTI International's 2023 LACA study (Chew et al.), GPT-3.5 'can often perform deductive coding at levels of agreement comparable to human coders'; on one dataset coding took about 4 seconds per document versus 144 for humans.
Acceptability reason: Methodologists endorse it when agreement is validated against human-coded samples; studies show weak performance on rare codes.
Advantages:
• Agreement often comparable to human coders, at ~4 s vs 144 s per document (Chew et al., LACA, 2023)
• LACA helps refine prompts and flag codes where the LLM is guessing (Chew et al., 2023)
Disadvantages:
• LLMs fell short on rare, imbalanced codes compared with small fine-tuned classifiers (Li et al., 2025)
• Annotation errors can be systematically biased by interviewee characteristics (Ashwin et al., 2023)

Description: While a researcher codes transcripts manually, the tool suggests tags for each passage, learned from the researcher's own existing tags. It sits inside the normal manual coding step rather than replacing it. NN/g's 2023 evaluation observed an 'AI collaborator' tool surfacing AI-suggested tags at the top of the tag list when researchers coded transcripts.
Acceptability reason: Interview studies with qualitative researchers find this human-initiated, assistive delegation is the form they most accept because they keep ownership.

Description: An AI chatbot or purpose-built tool reads interview transcripts or other qualitative text and proposes codes (labels for meaningful passages) and themes without a predefined list. It sits right after transcription, as a first pass before the researcher reviews, merges and rewrites themes. In a CHI EA 2024 user study, ten qualitative researchers used ChatGPT for thematic analysis and found it sped up coding and initial data exploration but raised trust and consistency concerns.
Acceptability reason: NN/g and the CHI/arXiv literature accept it only as a first pass with human verification and interpretation; NN/g explicitly warns not to outsource analysis to AI.

Description: Here the AI drafts the codebook itself: the list of codes, their definitions and examples that researchers then apply to data. Text excerpts go in; the pipeline summarizes them, embeds and clusters similar points, and has an LLM name and define candidate codes and themes. It is used early in analysis to bootstrap a coding scheme for large datasets. The GATOS workflow (Purdue, 2026) used an open-weight model and text embeddings to approximate inductive codebook development and compared generated themes with original ones.
Acceptability reason: Academic authors present it as a support for researcher judgment that must be evaluated against human codes, not a replacement.
Advantages:
• Scales inductive codebook development to large datasets (Main et al., GATOS, 2026)
• Open-weight models allow local processing of sensitive data (Main et al., GATOS, 2026)
Disadvantages:
• Evaluated largely on synthetic datasets, limiting real-world validity (Main et al., GATOS, 2026)
• Researchers frequently had to verify, critique and rework outputs (Sharma et al., DeTAILS, 2025)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 0 built-in tools, 0 independent reports → insufficient evidence. Not fully re-verified in the October 2026 update; re-check in Run 3.

Description: The AI reads many sessions at once and outputs a list of 'insights' and recommendations for the whole study. Multiple transcripts (and in some tools behavioral data) go in; a ranked set of findings and suggested fixes comes out, ideally linked to evidence clips. It aims to shortcut the step from coded data to findings. NN/g's 2023 test of such tools on a real usability study found vague recommendations like 'provide more detailed descriptions' compared with specific human findings.
Acceptability reason: Vendors market it as evidence-backed, while NN/g found vague, context-blind output and warns that outsourcing analysis risks researcher credibility.
Advantages:
• Insights link back to source video for verification (UserTesting blog, 2023)
• Speeds up getting to an overview across many sessions (Lyssna 2025: 61% of AI users identify patterns)
Disadvantages:
• Vague, non-actionable recommendations and lack of study context (NN/g, Liu & Moran, 2023)
• Outsourcing analysis risks bad insights and credibility (NN/g, Maria Rosala video)
Popularity basis: Survey: 32.4% of all respondents → medium (16–50%).
Survey source: Maze Future of User Research Report 2026, synthesis and reporting, 47% of AI users × 69% (vendor-run)
Independent reports: UX research trends 2026 (Lyssna) — https://www.lyssna.com/blog/ux-research-trends/

Use case: Turning themes into insights and recommendations
Description: After themes are identified, the AI drafts insight statements, recommendations or 'How Might We' prompts. Themes and supporting quotes go in, and draft insight or action statements come out for the researcher to edit. This is the hand-off from analysis to synthesis. Lyssna's 2025 survey found that 47.6% of practitioners who use AI use it to translate insights into recommendations.
Acceptability reason: Research-platform reports and NN/g treat AI as a 'thought partner' in synthesis, with spot-checks against the raw data. I found no peer-reviewed evaluation of the quality of AI-written insights or HMW questions.
Advantages: • Widely adopted: 47.6% of AI users translate insights into recommendations (Lyssna 2025)
Disadvantages:
• Only 32% of respondents say they can rely on AI output (Figma 2025 AI report)
• I found no credible evaluation of the quality of AI-written HMW questions
Popularity basis: Survey: 26% of all respondents → medium (16–50%).

Tool categories: Design and whiteboard tools | General AI assistants
Description: The AI writes a first draft of a customer journey map, which shows the stages a person goes through and their actions, thoughts and feelings at each stage. The designer provides a persona, the journey to map, its stages and the research dataset. The AI fills in each stage, and the designer checks and refines it. Soucy's prompt template lists who is on the journey, which journey it is, its stages, and what to include at each stage (for example actions, thoughts and jobs-to-be-done). NN/g notes that synthetic data can produce 'proto journey maps' for early team alignment.
Acceptability reason: Soucy and NN/g accept AI for drafts or proto-maps when they are grounded in real research. Both explicitly reject fabricating maps.
Advantages:
• Turns synthesized insights into a deliverable quickly (Kyle Soucy)
• Useful for proto journey maps and hypotheses (NN/g)
Disadvantages:
• Generative AI may insert its own assumptions (Kyle Soucy, UXPA Boston 2025)
• Maps built from synthetic data are not suitable for final decisions (NN/g)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 1 built-in tool, 1 independent report → low.
Independent reports: Synthetic Users (NN/g, proto journey maps) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/synthetic-users/

Tool categories: General AI assistants | Design and whiteboard tools | Research platforms
Description: The AI writes user personas, which are short profiles of typical users. Designers upload research notes, transcripts or survey data and define the persona sections they want. The AI drafts each persona's goals, frustrations and behaviours, and the designer reviews and edits the draft. This step comes after analysis, when findings are turned into a shareable artifact. Kyle Soucy describes uploading real research data to ChatGPT or Claude with a structured prompt, then checking the output for assumptions the AI has made.
Acceptability reason: Practitioners such as Soucy and NN/g accept AI drafting only when it is grounded in real data and reviewed by a person. HCI audits show that personas generated without data come out stereotyped.
Advantages:
• Faster first drafts from uploaded research (Kyle Soucy)
• AI personas were rated more informative, consistent and clear than personas written by novices (Lazik et al., HU Berlin)
Disadvantages:
• AI personas were significantly more positive and stereotypical (Lazik et al.)
• LLM personas foreground racial markers, a pattern the authors call 'algorithmic othering' (Venkit et al., Penn State)
• A scoping review of 81 articles found 45% lack any evaluation and 86% use only GPT models (Amin, Salminen, Jansen et al.)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 1 built-in tool, 2 independent reports → low.

Tool categories: General AI assistants | Design and whiteboard tools
Description: An empathy map is a four-part board showing what users say, think, do and feel. Here the AI is asked to fill it in. Designers either prompt the AI to invent user quotes and emotions, or feed it real research notes to organize. NN/g separates the two cases. Organizing real notes and tidying their wording is acceptable. Generating quotes, behaviours or emotions for users who do not exist, or filling gaps in thin research, is not.
Acceptability reason: NN/g (Rachel Krause, 2026) states that 'AI-generated data is not evidence' and that AI should not generate user content for empathy maps. Only organizing real data is acceptable.
Advantages: • Can help organize and cluster notes from research already collected (NN/g)
Disadvantages:
• Invents quotes and emotions for users who do not exist (NN/g)
• Plausible-sounding filler can hide thin research (NN/g)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 0 built-in tools, 0 independent reports → insufficient evidence.

Description: A persona is turned into a chatbot that designers can talk to. Persona details or research data go in. The LLM role-plays the persona, answering questions, reacting to ideas and giving 'user-like' feedback in real time. Designers use it while ideating and refining concepts, in place of reading a static persona document. In a study by Deep et al., eight professional UX designers interviewed and brainstormed with a voice persona called 'Alice'.
Acceptability reason: HCI researchers report benefits for engagement and inspiration. The same studies and NN/g warn about bias, over-optimism and invented detail, and say these chatbots should complement real users, not replace them.
Advantages:
• Speeds up information gathering and inspires solutions (Deep et al., IJHCS 2025)
• Could increase empathy for users with complex needs (Sun et al., Persona-L)
Disadvantages:
• Designers flagged bias and over-optimism: 'She was useful, but a bit too optimistic' (Deep et al.)
• The interactive format raised designers' expectations of what the persona should know (AI EDAM 'Synthetic users' study)
• NN/g found synthetic users give 'shallow or overly favorable feedback'
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 0 built-in tools, 1 independent report → low.
Independent reports: Synthetic Users: If, When, and How (NN/g) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/synthetic-users/

Description: Before analysis or sharing, AI finds and removes personal information such as names, emails or card numbers from raw research data. Transcripts, audio and video go in; text is redacted and media blurred or muted, optionally as suggestions to review. It is a data-preparation step at the start of analysis that protects participants. Dovetail's 2026 changelog describes a workspace-level prompt that detects sensitive information, with a Suggest mode for reviewing proposed redactions.
Acceptability reason: NN/g rates cleaning and sanitizing data as an AI capability that protects participants and reduces tedious work, with checks for mistakes.
Advantages:
• Protects participant data and reduces tedious work (NN/g, Moran & Rosala)
• Suggest mode allows human review before applying (Dovetail changelog, 2026)
Disadvantages:
• Mistakes possible in detection (NN/g, Moran & Rosala)
• Enterprise-plan feature in Dovetail, limiting access (Dovetail docs)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 1 built-in tool, 0 independent reports → low.

Description: AI condenses a single interview or test session into key points, often with timestamps linked to the recording. A transcript (and sometimes notes) goes in; a short structured summary comes out. It is used immediately after each session to orient the team before deeper analysis. In Lyssna's Research Synthesis Report 2025 (300 professionals, May 2025), 82.9% of AI users generated summaries of key findings and 61.0% used AI to identify patterns.
Acceptability reason: NN/g rates summarizing interviews as a capability AI handles well for language-based data, with checks for misunderstandings or omissions.
Advantages:
• Most-used AI analysis task, reflecting strong time savings (User Interviews 2024: 73%; Lyssna 2025: 82.9% of AI users)
• Linked timestamps help verify points against the source (NN/g)
Disadvantages:
• Misunderstandings, omissions and higher error rates for some accents (NN/g)
• Summaries can be extremely vague (NN/g, Liu & Moran, 2023)
Popularity basis: Survey: 45.3% of all respondents → medium (16–50%).

Description: An opportunity solution tree is a diagram that links a desired outcome to the customer needs ('opportunities') heard in interviews, and then to possible solutions. Interview transcripts go in. The AI first drafts an 'interview snapshot' for each interview (key moments and opportunities), then combines the snapshots into a first-draft tree. Product teams use it during continuous discovery to decide what to work on next. Torres reports that a customer reviewing her first AI tree wanted to 'clean up this branch', which led her to build evals and repair loops.
Acceptability reason: Teresa Torres, who created the method, endorses AI drafting with human review. She notes that one badly framed opportunity corrupts every layer above it (the 'house of cards' problem).
Advantages: • Cuts the time needed to create interview snapshots, which Torres identified as a real pain point (Teresa Torres, Product Talk)
Disadvantages:
• Errors at the snapshot layer corrupt the tree built on top of it (Torres/Vistaly podcast)
• The evidence comes from the method's creator, who has a commercial partnership with the tool
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 0 built-in tools, 1 independent report → low.
Independent reports: Product Talk (Teresa Torres) on AI-generated opportunity solution trees — https://www.producttalk.org/
Resource 1: Generating Opportunity Solution Trees with AI: How Vistaly Rebuilt Its Product Around Interview Synthesis, Evals, and Repair Loops

Description: Reframing means recasting what a design problem is really about, for example treating 'slow elevators' as a 'frustrating wait'. The designer gives the AI the problem statement. The AI proposes alternative perspectives, or frames, and the designer picks or adapts one. This happens early in synthesis, before ideation. In Shin et al.'s CHI 2025 study, 280 designers tried three ways of working with LLMs, and none improved the quality of their frames.
Acceptability reason: Aalto researchers (CHI 2025) found no benefit and a wider gap between experienced and inexperienced designers. Ding et al. (C&C 2023) found that LLM analogies often changed how people formulated problems.
Advantages: • LLM analogies 'frequently (∼80% of cases) led to observable changes in problem formulations' (Ding, Srinivasan, MacNeil & Chan, C&C 2023)
Disadvantages:
• LLMs did not improve frame quality (Shin et al., CHI 2025)
• Widened the competence gap, and inexperienced designers felt less agency (Shin et al.)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 0 built-in tools, 0 independent reports → insufficient evidence. Not fully re-verified in the October 2026 update; re-check in Run 3.
Resource 1: No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing
Resource 2: Fluid Transformers and Creative Analogies

Description: An AI agent joins a group discussion to argue against the majority view or the leading idea. The group's discussion goes in, and the AI produces counterarguments and critical questions. It is used when design teams are converging on a concept, to surface overlooked concerns and give quieter members cover to disagree. Lee et al. (UNIST Department of Design) show the agent making it legitimate for a low-power member to dissent.
Acceptability reason: HCI researchers find value but stress that the timing of interventions and an adaptable role matter. Earlier work notes that counterarguments from an AI alone can feel inauthentic.
Advantages: • Creates productive disagreement and legitimizes minority views (Lee et al., UNIST)
Disadvantages:
• Poorly timed interventions disrupt the conversation (Lee et al.)
• The evidence comes from group decision tasks, not live design projects
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 0 built-in tools, 0 independent reports → insufficient evidence. Not fully re-verified in the October 2026 update; re-check in Run 3.
Resource 1: Conversational Agents as Catalysts for Critical Thinking: Challenging Social Influence in Group Decision-making

Description: The AI rates or shortlists ideas against criteria the team has agreed on. A list of ideas and a scorecard go in, and ratings and a shortlist come out. The team then debates the result. This step sits between generating ideas and selecting a concept. NN/g recommends a text scorecard so the LLM can rate each idea.
Acceptability reason: NN/g endorses it as an aid for narrowing ideas. A 2025 study found that selecting and evaluating ideas remains mostly done by people.
Advantages: • Makes very large sets of AI-generated ideas manageable (NN/g)
Disadvantages: • People still lead selection; AI mainly helps with problem definition and idea generation (arXiv 2502.00283)

Description: Participants write short speculative stories about possible futures while an AI suggests text. A theme goes in, the AI produces continuations, and the writers decide what to keep. Speculative designers use it to make futures concrete enough to discuss. In a workshop on 'future work in 2040', 20 young people in China responded to messy AI texts in ways that enriched their writing.
Acceptability reason: Design researchers (Wu, Yu, An) see creative value but recommend better design of the human–AI interaction and of prompting. The evidence is old and thin.
Advantages: • Unexpected AI texts made the writing richer and more creative, and made the process enjoyable (Wu et al.)
Disadvantages:
• The evidence pre-dates 2023 (Chinese CHI 2022) and involved non-designers
• Generated futures may carry model biases (raised in later DIS work, which I did not open)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 0 built-in tools, 0 independent reports → insufficient evidence. Not fully re-verified in the October 2026 update; re-check in Run 3.

Tool categories: General AI assistants | Design and whiteboard tools
Description: The designer uses a chatbot to generate many ideas, names or directions for a defined problem. A problem statement, or even a one-word prompt, goes in and lists of ideas come out. The designer then selects and combines them. This is the most widespread use in synthesis. NN/g notes that AI makes ideation 'virtually free' but that people must still select the ideas. Controlled studies show that ideas converge across users.
Acceptability reason: NN/g recommends AI as an ideation partner. Peer-reviewed studies (C&C 2024, CHI 2025) find that ideas become more alike across a group and that creativity without AI is weaker afterwards.
Advantages:
• Generates unlimited ideas with little effort (NN/g, AI for UX: Getting Started)
• Designers find it helpful for brainstorming tasks that don't need precision (NN/g)
Disadvantages:
• As a group, ChatGPT users produced ideas that were less semantically distinct from each other (Anderson, Shah, Kreminski, C&C 2024)
• Using diverse AI personas may reduce this effect (Wan & Kalman, 2025)
Popularity basis: Survey: 76% of all respondents → high (over 50%).

Tool categories: Design and whiteboard tools | General AI assistants
Description: Teams use AI during facilitated workshops to generate ideas and then narrow them down. Participants prompt the AI for many options; NN/g's Tanner Kohler asks for 15–20 per prompt. The AI then scores the options against agreed criteria, and the group discusses the shortlist. This adds an AI narrowing step to the classic diverge-then-converge structure. NN/g cites the P&G 'Cybernetic Teammate' field experiment (776 professionals): individuals with AI improved by 0.37 SD and teams with AI by 0.39 SD.
Acceptability reason: NN/g recommends it with facilitation safeguards: criteria scorecards, extra time for prompting, co-written prompts and digital documentation.
Advantages:
• Avoids groupthink and fixation on first ideas (NN/g)
• In the P&G experiment, a single person using AI matched a two-person team without AI (Dell'Acqua, Lakhani, Mollick et al., cited by NN/g)
Disadvantages:
• Too many ideas to process when the group converges (NN/g)
• Reading and prompt iteration take longer than expected (NN/g)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 3 built-in tools, 2 independent reports → medium.

Description: The AI suggests analogies from distant fields, such as biology, to inspire solutions. The designer enters a problem. The AI returns analogous mechanisms, and some tools also help map them onto the problem and weigh trade-offs. Designers use it to get out of obvious solution spaces during concept generation. BioSpark (Carnegie Mellon University and Toyota Research Institute) shows biological mechanisms to automobile concept designers in a Pinterest-like interface.
Acceptability reason: HCI researchers find the analogies often helpful, but some outputs are potentially harmful or inaccurate and need screening.
Advantages:
• Median helpfulness of 4 out of 5 (Ding et al.)
• Helps transfer mechanisms into the problem, not just find them (BioSpark, Kang et al.)
Disadvantages:
• 'An upper bound of ∼25% of outputs being rated as potentially harmful, with a majority due to potentially upsetting content' (Ding et al., C&C 2023)
• Text-based generative systems can cause fixation (Inkspire authors)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 0 built-in tools, 0 independent reports → insufficient evidence. Not fully re-verified in the October 2026 update; re-check in Run 3.

Text prompts or reference images go in, and many images or recombinations come out. Designers use these images to shape early concepts and sketches. This counts as Synthesis when the images inform concept direction, and as Prototype when they become a testable artifact. CreativeConnect (CHI 2024) helped 16 users produce more ideas, but a separate CHI 2024 experiment found that AI images increased fixation.

Disadvantages:
• Higher fixation, fewer ideas and lower originality (Wadinambiarachchi et al., CHI 2024)

Use case: Prototyping AI features with live models
Tools: Claude Code | Cursor | Figma Make | Lovable
Description: When the product being designed is itself an AI feature (a chatbot, voice assistant or on-screen helper), designers build prototypes that call a real language model so test participants experience actual AI behavior rather than scripted screens. In the CMU approach, designers replay recorded user-session videos to an LLM, refine its instructions, rate candidate responses, and in live 'hybrid Wizard-of-Oz' sessions a human approves AI responses before they reach the participant. The output is a tested prompt strategy and a prototype whose AI behavior has been checked in context. It sits at the boundary of making and testing, because the AI's responses are part of the artifact being evaluated. NN/g (2026) similarly notes that AI prototyping makes it feasible to include AI-generated responses in prototypes and test them with users before deployment, while cautioning that this shows what became feasible, not that the research is better.
Acceptability reason: CMU HCI researchers and NN/g both recommend prototyping AI behavior with real models and real users, because static mockups cannot anticipate the variability of AI output; they caution about limits rather than advising against it.
Advantages:
• Supports immersive, in-context evaluation of prompt strategies for real-time multimodal agents (Gmeiner, Holstein & Martelaro, CMU, arXiv 2025)
• Brings realistic AI responses into testable prototypes earlier in the process (NN/g, Megan Chan, 2026)
Disadvantages:
• Existing prototyping and evaluation methods were insufficient to anticipate the situational complexity of real-time agents; the replay approach has acknowledged limitations (Gmeiner et al., arXiv 2025)
• Feasibility of building such prototypes is not evidence that the resulting research is better (NN/g, Megan Chan, 2026)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 0 built-in tools, 1 independent report → low.
Independent reports: Figma 2025 AI report: Perspectives from designers and developers — https://www.figma.com/blog/figma-2025-ai-report-perspectives/

Tool categories: Prototyping and coding tools | Design and whiteboard tools
Description: Instead of describing a screen in words, the designer gives the AI a picture or file: a photo of a hand sketch, a mockup screenshot, or a link to a Figma frame. The AI reads the visual reference and writes HTML/CSS or app code that tries to reproduce it as a working page or prototype. It sits where design meets build: turning an existing sketch or mockup into something clickable, or into code a developer can start from. In NN/g's 2025 evaluation, prompts with an attached artifact produced more streamlined results, and when given a Figma frame link, Lovable and Replit came closest to the NN/g designer's original. The Design2Code benchmark (484 real webpages) found that frontier models still mostly lag in recalling visual elements and producing correct layouts.
Acceptability reason: NN/g recommends attaching references to get better prototypes, but both NN/g and the Design2Code authors show fidelity gaps, so output needs designer and developer review before it is treated as production-ready.
Advantages:
• Attaching a sketch, mockup or Figma frame yields more streamlined, more accurate outputs than text alone (NN/g, Wang & Brown, 2025)
• Turns existing design artifacts into interactive code-based prototypes quickly (NN/g evaluation methodology, 2025)
Disadvantages:
• Models mostly lag in recalling visual elements and generating correct layouts (Si et al., Design2Code, NAACL 2025)
• Generated code is unreliable and hard to integrate (Li et al., CHIWORK '26)
• Vendor pages describe 'production-ready' mockups and handoff code, a claim not supported by independent evaluations (Figma Make page vs. NN/g 2025)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 3 built-in tools, 1 independent report → low. Not fully re-verified in the October 2026 update; re-check in Run 3.

Tools: Claude Code | Cursor | Figma Make | Lovable | Bolt | Replit | v0 | OpenAI Codex
Tool categories: Prototyping and coding tools | General AI assistants
Description: Designers describe a product in natural language and an AI coding tool writes working front-end code, producing a clickable, often data-driven prototype that runs in a browser. The input is a prompt (often a written spec, screenshots or a Figma link); the AI generates the code and helps debug it over several rounds; the output is an interactive prototype that can be shared with stakeholders or put in front of test participants. It sits between static mockups and engineering, and NN/g (2026) highlights it for testing complex interfaces such as filters, dashboards and conversational AI. Example: the Paris design studio Source set up Lovable with a client's colors, fonts and components plus a structured PRD as a master prompt, and in three weeks two designers and an AI design engineer delivered two prototypes for a logistics tool. Designer Hardik Pandya reports spending 60 hours and about 1.5 billion tokens on one Cursor prototype without opening Figma.
Acceptability reason: NN/g and a CHIWORK '26 interview study support it for exploration, stakeholder demos and early user testing, but not as production code or as a substitute for design judgment.
Advantages:
• Accelerates iteration, supports creativity and lowers barriers to participation (Li et al., 22 interviews, CHIWORK '26)
• Makes it feasible to test realistic states, data and AI-generated responses with users earlier (NN/g, Megan Chan, 2026)
• Detailed prompts produce outputs that closely resemble human-designed versions (NN/g, Wang & Brown, 2025)
Disadvantages:
• Code unreliability, integration problems and AI over-reliance, plus deskilling and social stigma (Li et al., CHIWORK '26)
• Even close outputs miss nuance in spacing, grouping and hierarchy (NN/g, Wang & Brown, 2025)
• Prototypes break often and the LLM drifts or hallucinates (Hardik Pandya, product designer, first-hand)
Popularity basis: Survey: 62.3% of all respondents → high (over 50%).
Survey source: State of Prototyping Spring 2026, UX Tools (n=1,478; vendor-sponsored); AI in Design 2026 official page: 85% have used AI coding tools or app builders

Tools: Midjourney | Adobe Firefly | ChatGPT Images | Figma | Figma Weave
Tool categories: Image generation | Design and whiteboard tools
Description: AI generates or edits the pictures that go into a mockup or prototype, such as hero photos, illustrations and product imagery, instead of stock photography or gray placeholder boxes. The designer writes a prompt (or selects an image to edit, e.g., remove its background); the AI returns images that are placed into the design. This entry covers assets placed into tangible artifacts; mood boards for concept exploration were mapped earlier under Synthesis. In an NN/g study (2026), 77 US adults rated six versions of a webpage that differed only in the hero image (three made with ChatGPT Images 2.0, three stock photos); the AI images carried no penalty and scored slightly higher, with only a small authenticity difference reaching significance. NN/g's 2025 tool review named Midjourney among the narrow-scope tools that stood out.
Acceptability reason: NN/g found AI images perform as well as stock photos when users don't know their origin, but cautions this may change if users know or suspect AI, and disclosure rules now apply in some contexts.
Advantages:
• No perception penalty versus stock photos on trust, professionalism or authenticity when origin is undisclosed (NN/g, Rachel Banawa, 2026)
• Narrow image tools such as Midjourney are among the few design-specific AI tools NN/g found genuinely helpful (NN/g, Brown, Sponheim & Dykes, 2025)
Disadvantages:
• Findings rest on only six images in one industry and may not hold if users know or suspect AI generation (NN/g, Rachel Banawa, 2026)
• EU AI Act transparency obligations that began in August 2026 require disclosing AI-generated content in some cases (NN/g, Taylor Dykes, PACED framework, 2026)
• UX professionals use genAI far less for multimedia than for text (NN/g, AI as a UX Assistant)
Popularity basis: Survey: 44% of all respondents → medium (16–50%).
Survey source: AI in Design 2026, image or video generation (% from third-party transcription); Figma 2025 AI report 33% (vendor-run)

Tool categories: General AI assistants | Design and whiteboard tools
Description: AI drafts or rewrites the short text inside an interface, such as button labels, error messages, headings, empty states and onboarding copy. The designer explains where the text appears and what it must convey; the AI proposes one or more versions; the designer picks and edits them in the mockup or prototype. It sits in the making phase alongside layout work, often done by designers who are not trained writers. NN/g's practitioner FAQ calls AI 'genuinely useful' for first drafts, headline variations, alt text and microcopy brainstorming, but warns that output tends toward the generic and drifts from brand voice. One NN/g survey respondent, Florian Bölter, describes always telling the AI where the copy appears and what it needs to convey 'so AI knows all constraints'.
Acceptability reason: NN/g endorses AI as a 'first-draft collaborator' only on the condition that copy is always edited for the audience and never published without human review.
Advantages:
• Gets past the blank page and produces variations quickly (NN/g, UX Writing FAQs)
• Lets designers who are not writers adjust or generate copy in-canvas (NN/g, Brown, Sponheim & Dykes, 2025)
Disadvantages:
• Output tends toward the generic, drifts from brand voice and knows nothing about your users or research (NN/g, UX Writing FAQs)
• Generative AI can produce plausible-sounding but incorrect content (NN/g, AI as a UX Assistant)
Popularity basis: Survey: 70% of all respondents → high (over 50%).

Tool categories: Design and whiteboard tools | General AI assistants
Description: AI generates believable tables, chart data, names, avatars and text to replace 'lorem ipsum' and dummy numbers in prototypes that will be tested with people. The designer describes the audience, columns, value ranges and the story the data should tell; the AI produces structured data that is imported into the design tool or prototype code; the result is a prototype that feels real to test participants. It sits just before usability testing, raising content fidelity. NN/g's Evan Sunwall (2024) notes that participants scrutinize tables and charts whether you want them to or not, offers seven tactics each for mock tables and charts, and found Claude 3.5 Sonnet more reliable than ChatGPT-4o for the job. Designer Hardik Pandya reports Cursor generating a table UI with realistic names, companies and timestamps in under 10 seconds.
Acceptability reason: NN/g recommends it, with normal care: follow organizational data policy and never share sensitive or identifying data with unapproved AI tools.
Advantages:
• Removes a time-consuming chore and improves content fidelity for usability testing (NN/g, Evan Sunwall, 2024)
• Survey respondents recommend AI text and images in prototypes instead of 'lorem ipsum' (NN/g, AI for UX: Getting Started)
• Fast generation of realistic people, companies and timestamps (Hardik Pandya, practitioner)
Disadvantages:
• Risk of exposing real or sensitive data when seeding prompts with examples (NN/g, Evan Sunwall, 2024)
• AI features embedded in design tools may generate tables and charts less effectively than general-purpose chatbots (NN/g, Evan Sunwall, 2024)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 1 built-in tool, 1 independent report → low. Not fully re-verified in the October 2026 update; re-check in Run 3.

Description: AI helps designers find existing components, icons, screens and files by showing an example instead of remembering exact names. The input is a screenshot, a selected frame, a quick pencil sketch, or descriptive keywords; the AI matches it against team files and libraries; the output is a list of similar designs or components to reuse. It sits in design-system and component work, encouraging reuse rather than redrawing. NN/g (2025) highlights 'Find more like' as removing the stress of digging through files across projects and teams, finding missing or related assets 'almost instantly'. Figma describes the search as understanding context, so assets turn up even when search terms don't match their names.
Acceptability reason: NN/g lists it among the narrow-scope Figma AI features that are meaningfully helpful for designers.
Advantages:
• Finds missing or related assets almost instantly from keywords, images or layer selections (NN/g, Brown, Sponheim & Dykes, 2025)
• Works even when search terms don't match asset names (Figma, Config 2024 – vendor description)
Disadvantages:
• Searches only team files the user has access to (Figma, Config 2024)
• No independent accuracy measurement found; evidence is NN/g's qualitative review plus vendor description (gap noted in this scan)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 1 built-in tool, 1 independent report → low. Not fully re-verified in the October 2026 update; re-check in Run 3.

Description: AI gives meaningful names to the layers in a design file (for example turning 'Frame 14353411' into 'Songs'), which keeps files and design systems tidy. The designer selects layers or a whole frame; the AI looks at each layer's content, position and relationship to neighboring layers; it renames them in bulk. It sits in the housekeeping part of making, before handoff or sharing with teammates. NN/g (2025) says the tool 'completely eliminates the tedious task of renaming layers' and makes layers easier to search. A LogRocket guide (2026) adds that duplicates in other frames are renamed consistently so prototypes keep working, while hidden, locked or nested-instance layers are skipped.
Acceptability reason: NN/g counts it among the narrow-scope AI features that are genuinely helpful and actually adopted for everyday work, with no credible objections found.
Advantages:
• Eliminates a tedious, often-skipped task and makes layers searchable (NN/g, Brown, Sponheim & Dykes, 2025)
• Keeps duplicate layers consistent so prototype connections continue to work (LogRocket, Bart Krawczyk, 2026)
Disadvantages:
• Skips hidden, locked, nested-instance and vector layers, which must be renamed manually (LogRocket, Bart Krawczyk, 2026)
• Adds metadata only; an efficiency gain rather than an improvement in design quality (NN/g, Brown, Sponheim & Dykes, 2025)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 1 built-in tool, 1 independent report → low. Not fully re-verified in the October 2026 update; re-check in Run 3.

Tools: Figma Make | Claude Code | Cursor | Magic Patterns
Tool categories: Prototyping and coding tools | Design and whiteboard tools
Description: The AI is given a team's existing components, colors, fonts and brand rules so that the screens or prototypes it generates reuse them, instead of inventing a generic look. The input is a design library or a pre-configured 'starter kit' plus written rules; the AI composes new screens from those parts; the output is a mockup or prototype that looks like the real product. It sits at the point where generation meets design-system work, making AI drafts usable with real stakeholders. NN/g (2025) states that AI needs to pull from established design systems to create a cohesive look and that Figma and its competitors are still working towards it. For a logistics client, Source.paris built a Lovable environment aligned with the client's brand charter plus precise rules, because presenting generic screens to decision-makers was 'out of the question'.
Acceptability reason: NN/g treats design-system grounding as a precondition for useful AI design output and reports tools were not yet there in 2025; practitioners report it works only with deliberate setup and rules.
Advantages:
• Lets exploratory prototypes match the client's visual language, making them credible to decision-makers (Source.paris, consultancy case)
• Addresses the generic-look problem NN/g identified in AI outputs (NN/g, Brown, Sponheim & Dykes, 2025)
Disadvantages:
• Tools were still 'working towards' design-system integration, and limited context windows may block it (NN/g, Brown, Sponheim & Dykes, 2025)
• Requires substantial upfront preparation of kits and rules (Source.paris)
• The vendor claim that Make 'pulls from your existing Figma design system' is not independently evaluated (Figma Make product page)
Popularity basis: No task-specific survey; 1 built-in tool, 1 independent report → low.

Tools: Figma Make | Figma | Google Stitch | Uizard | v0 | Lovable | Claude Design
Tool categories: Design and whiteboard tools | Prototyping and coding tools
Description: A designer types a plain-language description of a screen or app and the AI returns editable static wireframes or high-fidelity mockups. The input is a text prompt (sometimes plus a chosen starting library, such as 'app wireframe' or 'basic app' in Figma First Draft); the model assembles layouts, components and placeholder content; the output is one or more screens on the design canvas. It sits at the very start of making, replacing the blank canvas with a first draft that the designer then edits by hand. In NN/g's 2025 evaluation, prompting First Draft for an NN/g profile page produced a result that was generic, with poor information and visual hierarchy even for a wireframe. In a week-long diary study, 37 UX designers, researchers, PMs and engineers summed up the tool as a 'good first draft, tough last mile'.
Acceptability reason: NN/g (2024, 2025) and the authors of the DIS '25 GenUI study treat it as useful only for early exploration and visual communication, because outputs are generic and need heavy revision by a designer.
Advantages:
• Saves time and effort on the first draft and supports early ideation and visual communication across roles (Chen, Knearem & Li, GenUI study, DIS '25)
• Open-ended prompts can surface unexpected layout directions that are useful in early exploration (NN/g, Wang & Brown, 2025)
Disadvantages:
• Outputs are generic, with poor information and visual hierarchy (NN/g, Brown, Sponheim & Dykes, 2025)
• NN/g's 2024 interviews found zero design-specific AI tools in serious use by professional UX designers (NN/g, Sponheim & Brown, 2024)
• Without detailed specs, tools converge on a similar generic look, a homogenization risk (NN/g, Wang & Brown, 2025)
Popularity basis: Survey: 43% of all respondents → medium (16–50%).
Survey source: AI in Design 2026, wireframing (+27 pts confirmed on official page; % from third-party transcription); Figma 2025 AI report 22% (vendor-run)
